Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Discuss the importance of clinical history and patient factors guiding the differential diagnosis
of bone and soft-tissue tumor mimickers.
Identify the characteristics (location and pattern) of soft-tissue mineralization of benign versus
malignant processes.
Describe the radiographic appearance, underlying pathophysiology, and management of
metabolic bone disease.
Perform an appropriate workup of soft-tissue and bone neoplasms.

Introduction

Nonneoplastic conditions, including metabolic disease, normal physiologic changes, infection,
inflammatory and autoimmune disease, trauma, and normal radiographic variants, may mimic
bone and soft-tissue tumors.

Introduction
Appropriate clinical history, physical examination, and radiographic and laboratory
findings may expedite the diagnosis of these conditions. Early recognition of the correct
diagnosis may minimize patient anxiety, maximize cost-effective workup by reducing
unnecessary tests and/or invasive procedures, and facilitate timely management of the
underlying condition if applicable. Unfortunately, these may be challenging diagnoses to
make, especially if an associated underlying medical condition has not been previously
diagnosed.
Evaluation
Clinical history, including systemic/constitutional symptoms; personal and family medical
history; trauma, tobacco and alcohol use; and medications.
Physical examination should focus on the identification of multiple organ system involvement,
alternative local sources for pain, and overlying skin changes.
Laboratory tests should be tailored based on the suspected diagnosis but may include the
following:
Inflammatory markers: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein level
Complete blood count
Basic metabolic panel
Factors associated with calcium homeostasis (calcium, vitamin D, parathyroid hormone
levels)
Alkaline phosphatase level
Imaging studies typically include plain radiographs that may be diagnostic; however, CT and
MRI may play a role.
Bone Pseudotumors and Tumorlike Lesions
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520

Normal Radiographic Variants
Secondary to variable radiographic rarefaction, trabecular patterns, or rotational views, classic
radiolucent areas may be mistaken for bone lesions.
Humerus
Humeral Pseudocyst
Radiolucent lesion in the proximal humerus, adjacent to the greater tuberosity (Figure 1 and
2)
Figure 1 Radiograph (A) and photograph (B) of the corona section of a proximal humerus
show the characteristics of humeral pseudocyst. The area of rarefaction adjacent to the
greater tuberosity is well visualized. The curvilinear inferior margin (arrowheads) represents a
distinct band of trabeculae that separate the relatively porous region laterally and the more
compact spongiosa medially. A\ fusion line, marking the site of closure of a portion of the
physis, is faintly visible (open arrow). (Reproduced with permission from Resnick D, Cone RO
III: The nature of humeral pseudocysts. Radiology 1984;150[1]:27-28.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
3/48

Figure 2 Chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral humeral pseudocysts. These are not true
lesions but areas of rarefaction in the proximal humerus; therefore, the finding is observed
bilaterally. (Reproduced from Abraham JA: Benign radiolucent lesions, in Biermann JS, Siegel
GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 99-109.)
A well-defined inferior margin commonly is observed; however, the superior margin usually is
less well defined.
More apparent in younger patients because loss of trabecular bone with aging causes
decreased juxtaposition between the denser metaphyseal bone and the less-dense bone of
the greater tuberosity.1
May be present in the contralateral humeral head
Radiographs should be examined critically to assess for more aggressive features, such as
cortical destruction, periosteal reaction, matrix mineralization, or soft-tissue extension.
Humeral Head Internal Rotation View
With internal rotation of the shoulder, the humeral head may be superimposed such that an
apparent sclerotic border may be observed surrounding the relatively lucent trabecular bone
of the humeral head.
This is not observed on AP and Grashey views.2
SEND FEEDBACK

Radius
Radial Tuberosity Lateral View
The radial tuberosity may appear as a radiolucent lesion on plain radiographs of the forearm
or elbow if the x-ray beam is perfectly in line with the radial tuberosity of the proximal radius.
This may be mistaken for a bone lesion; however, the lucent appearance disappears with
views in other planes.
Femur
Ward Triangle
Radiolucent lesion with an etiology similar to that of a humeral pseudocyst
An area of less dense trabecular bone in the proximal femur
Formed as a result of the juxtaposition adjacent to the denser compressive and tensile
trabeculae (Figure 3)
Figure 3 AP radiograph of a right proximal femur demonstrates the internal weight-bearing
system in the femoral neck. I = intertrochanteric arch, L = lateral system of lamellae, M =
medial system of lamellae, W = Ward triangle. (Reproduced with permission from Garden RS:

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
5/48

The structure and function of the proximal end of the femur. J Bone Joint Surg Br
1961;43[3]:576-589.)
Ludloff Spot
Radiolucent lesion in the central region of the distal femur; frequently obscured by the patella3
(Figure 4).
Figure 4 AP radiograph of the distal femur of a paleopathologic specimen demonstrates a
region of lucency between the medial and lateral femoral condyle (arrowheads). (Reproduced
with permission from De Wilde V, De Maeseneer M, Lenchik L, Van Roy P, Beeckman P,
Osteaux M: Normal osseous variants presenting as cystic or lucent areas on radiography and
CT imaging: A pictorial overview. Eur J Radiol 2004;51[1]:77-84.)
Calcaneus
Calcaneal Pseudocyst
The calcaneus is an infrequent location for benign bone tumors; however, various benign
tumors may involve the calcaneus.
These include unicameral bone cysts, intraosseous lipoma, aneurysmal bone cysts,
chondroblastoma, and chondromyxofibroma.
Most common are unicameral bone cysts and intraosseous lipomas that present as
radiolucent lesions in the base of the calcaneal neck (Figure 5).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
6/48

This location also is the site of another pseudocyst, again produced by the rarefaction
phenomenon.
Compared with unicameral bone cysts and intraosseous lipomas, calcaneal pseudocysts
typically have an ill-defined border.4
Figure 5 Lateral radiograph of the calcaneus of a paleopathologic specimen demonstrates a
normal area of lucency in the anterior aspect of calcaneus (star). (Reproduced with permission
from De Wilde V, De Maeseneer M, Lenchik L, Van Roy P, Beeckman P, Osteaux M: Normal
osseous variants presenting as cystic or lucent areas on radiography and CT imaging: A pictorial
overview. Eur J Radiol 2004;51[1]:77-84.)
Bone-Forming Pseudotumors
Enostosis
Oval or round sclerotic lesions within the medullary cavity formed by dense compact bone
Commonly present as incidental findings; however, they must be differentiated from other
sclerotic lesions.
CT scans show normal surrounding trabecular bone adjacent to the bone island (enostosis)
MRIs show low-intensity signal on T1- and T2-weighted images without evidence of perilesional
edema.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
7/48

These lesions only require recognition and differentiation from more aggressive lesions; they
do not require management.
Radiographically, they appear as homogenous, dense sclerotic lesions within the cancellous
bone (Figure 6).
Figure 6 AP hip radiograph demonstrates a bone island of the iliac wing (arrow) discovered
incidentally. This very dense bone lesion is characterized by a geographic, smooth border;
intramedullary location; and homogeneous density throughout the lesion. (Reproduced from
Henshaw RM, Carmody EE: Benign bone-forming tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 125-140.)
Osteopoikilosis
Also known as spotted bone disease and presents as multiple sclerotic bone lesions
distributed throughout the skeletal system (Figure 7)
Radiographically resemble enostoses; however, in general, are between 2 and 10 mm in size.
Caused by a germline mutation in LEMD3, which is involved in regulation of SMAD signaling5
These lesions do not require management, only recognition and differentiation from
osteoblastic metastatic bone disease.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
8/48

Figure 7 Axial CT scans of the hips (A) and pelvis (B) of a 20-year-old man show classic
osteopoikilosis (spotted bone disease) involving multiple bones. (Reproduced from Henshaw
RM, Carmody EE: Benign bone-forming tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds: Orthopaedic
Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 125-140.)
Melorheostosis
Dissimilar from enostoses and many other bone tumor mimickers, melorheostosis typically
presents as symptoms, including pain, swelling, deformity, joint contracture, and nerve
entrapment syndrome.5
Radiographically, these lesions are characterized by sclerotic, thickened, cortical bone.
Localized to the medial or lateral side
May affect multiple adjacent bones
May affect the endosteal or periosteal surface
If it affects the periosteal surface, its appearance is described as dripping candle wax (Figure
8).
Soft tissues overlying the lesion may be fibrotic or edematous or have other cutaneous
changes.5
If monostotic disease is present, differentiation from other bone-producing surface lesions,
such as osteoid osteoma and parosteal osteosarcoma, may be difficult.
Surgical management may be required for the resultant deformities and soft-tissue
contractures.
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520

Figure 8 AP radiographs of the leg (A) and foot (B) of a patient with extensive melorheostosis
involving multiple bones shows the dense, homogeneous cortical hyperostosis of this
disease, which results in its classic dripping candle wax appearance. (Reproduced from
Henshaw RM, Carmody EE: Benign bone-forming tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 125-140.)
Marrow Changes, Irradiation-Induced Reactions, and Bone Infarcts
Plain radiographic changes often are subtle, whereas MRI features may be more easily
appreciated.
Red Marrow Conversion
Red marrow is a highly vascularized, active marrow.
Red marrow is converted to yellow marrow with increasing age; compared with red marrow,
yellow marrow has very little vascularity and hematopoietic activity.
In addition, because of the increased cellularity and hematopoietic activity, red marrow
demonstrates greater contrast enhancement and fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
10/48

tomography avidity than yellow marrow.
Persistent red marrow in adults typically is metaphyseal and has a flame pattern.
Red marrow conversion may be observed in patients with hemolytic anemia, heavy menstrual
cycles, and obesity and in endurance athletes, patients being treated with granulocyte colony-
stimulating factor, and smokers because of increased oxygen demands.6

Red Marrow Conversion
Because of the low-fat content of red marrow, red marrow appears isointense to muscle
on T1-weighted MRIs. As red marrow is converted to yellow marrow, the marrow
becomes more intense on T1-weighted MRIs. Because of the water content of red
marrow, red marrow appears hyperintense to skeletal muscle on T2-weighted fat-
saturated and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) MRIs (Figure 9).
Figure 9 Fat-saturated T2-weighted (A) and proton density (B) sagittal MRIs of a knee of
an 18-year-old patient show normal red marrow residua in the extremity long bones.
These residua appear in the distal femur and proximal tibia metaphyses as flame-shape
foci with feathery margins and slightly higher signal intensity than skeletal muscle.
(Reproduced with permission from Guillerman RP: Marrow: red, yellow and bad. Pediatr
Radiol 2013;43[suppl 1]:S181-S192.)
Irradiation-Induced Reactions
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
11/48

Background
Radiation therapy induces adverse changes in irradiated tissues, and bone is particularly
susceptible. Radiation therapy may produce striking changes within the bone.
If observed out of the context of prior radiation therapy, these changes may be concerning,
particularly for metastatic bone disease.
Irradiation-associated osseous changes include irradiation osteitis and osteoradionecrosis.
The extent and degree of radiation therapy depends on the volume of bone, delivery
mechanism, total dose, and patient-related factors that affect preexisting bone health.7
Etiology
Radiation therapy induces a toxic response in bone, leading to increased endothelial
permeability, interstitial edema, cellular swelling, and ultimately death of bone marrow cells.
Leads to degradation of bone and osteonecrosis
More common in patients who receive doses greater than 40 Gy7
Imaging Studies
Acute irradiation osteitis changes may transition to osteoradionecrosis in approximately 15%
of patients.7
Radiation osteitis
Hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, occasionally
marked confluent contrast enhancement7
Osteoradionecrosis:
Central hypointensity and peripheral hyperintensity on T1-weighted images, isointense- to
hypointense centrally with peripheral hyperintensity, halo-like contrast enhancement pattern
on T2-weighted images7
Management
Management primarily is limited to recognition that these radiographic changes are secondary
to radiation therapy and not metastatic disease or other primary bone tumors.
Fractures involving irradiated bone may be notoriously difficult to manage and are associated
with a high risk for nonunion.
Bone Infarction
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
12/48

Etiology and Epidemiology
Develops secondary to bone marrow ischemia and ultimately cell death; however, the exact
pathophysiology is unknown.
Bone infarcts are not uncommon and are associated with sickle cell anemia, tobacco abuse,
chronic steroid use, alcohol abuse, Gaucher disease, lupus, and renal transplantation.
Typically, bone infarction is incidentally identified and does not cause pain.
Imaging Studies
Radiographic and MRI appearance is highly dependent on the timing of the development of
the lesion. Bone infarcts tend to be located in the metaphyseal region of long bones, most
commonly the distal femur and the proximal tibia.
Radiographs
Early on, the lesions may be radiolucent with no clear evidence of a lesion radiographically.
As the lesions mature, the typical pattern is that of a normal-appearing bone with an
intramedullary lesion with central necrosis and a sclerotic serpentine border.
Often described radiographically as smoke in the chimney, in which the thick cortex
represents the chimney. A mature periosteal reaction may be present (Figure 10).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
13/48

Figure 10 AP knee radiographs demonstrate bone infarct. A, Radiograph of a knee
demonstrates a linear and circular pattern of bone sclerosis in the distal femur and proximal
tibia consistent with a bone infarct. B, Radiograph of the knee of a 19-year-old previously
treated for leukemia demonstrates a mature periosteal reaction along the medial distal
femur (arrow). (Reproduced from Avedian RS: Pseudotumors and tumorlike lesions, in
Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds. Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 43-55.)
MRI
On T1-weighted images, the sclerotic bone has a low signal intensity, which may appear as a
low or high signal intensity on T2-weighted images.
The region between these bands is high intensity on T1-weighted images, consistent with
normal marrow fat. Peripheral contrast enhancement may be present (Figure 11).
A periosteal reaction may be evident on MRI.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
14/48

Figure 11 Coronal T1-weighted MRI of the knee shown in Figure 10, B shows a serpiginous
medullar lesion with a low signal perimeter and a fat signal internally. The radiographic and
MRI findings are characteristic of a bone infarct. (Reproduced from Avedian RS:
Pseudotumors and tumorlike lesions, in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds. Orthopaedic Knowledge
Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 43-55.)
Management
Patients with a bone infarct generally are asymptomatic and require recognition of the
disease.
Very rarely, a secondary sarcoma may arise from these lesions.8
Trauma-Related Bone Lesions
Stress Reactions and Fractures
Stress-related bone changes may present as radiographically aggressive lesions with a
periosteal reaction in patients with pain. These most commonly involve the lower extremities
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
15/48

in active individuals; however, some patients may have a nontypical presentation.
Radiographic Appearance
Radiographs frequently demonstrate a confluent and extensive periosteal reaction.
An incomplete fracture line may not be apparent (Figure 12).
Figure 12 Radiographs of the tibia and fibula of a 23-year-old female professional basketball
player with an anterior tibial stress fracture. The fracture is not visible on an AP radiograph (A);
however, the black line (arrow), which represents an anterior tibia stress fracture, is observed
on a lateral radiograph (B). C, Magnification of the lateral radiograph demonstrates the black
line (arrow). (Reproduced from Shindle MK, Endo Y, Warren RF, et al: Stress fractures about the
tibia, foot, and ankle. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[3]:167-176.)
MRI reveals considerable endosteal and periosteal edema on STIR (Figure 13) and fat-
saturated T2-weighted images.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
16/48

T1-weighted MRIs may demonstrate a low signal intensity linear abnormality that represents a
fracture.
This is distinguished from a neoplastic process by the absence of a bone-replacing lesion with
normal surrounding marrow fat.
Figure 13 Axial short tau inversion recovery MRI obtained through the midshaft of a tibia
shows endosteal marrow edema (arrow) and periosteal edema (arrowhead) associated with a
tibial stress fracture. (Reproduced from Shindle MK, Endo Y, Warren RF, et al: Stress fractures
about the tibia, foot, and ankle. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[3]:167-176. )
Technetium-99m–labeled diphosphonate bone scans may demonstrate nonspecific focal
radiotracer uptake at the site of the stress reaction or fracture9 (Figure 14).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
17/48

Figure 14 Technetium-99m–labeled methylene diphosphonate bone scan of bilateral anterior
tibiae show focal tracer uptake in the lateral aspect of the midshaft of the right tibia, which is
consistent with a stress fracture. (Reproduced from Shindle MK, Endo Y, Warren RF, et al:
Stress fractures about the tibia, foot, and ankle. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[3]:167-176.)
Management
Management of stress reactions and fractures is highly dependent on the location.10
The most important aspect of management is recognition and differentiation from neoplastic
processes to facilitate timely referral and management.
Avulsive Cortical Irregularity
Avulsive cortical irregularities are cortically based lesions that occur at tendinous insertions.
These are reactive lesions secondary to traction or avulsions of tendons at their insertions.
These lesions also have been referred to as tug lesions; periosteal, subperiosteal, or cortical
desmoids; subperiosteal or cortical abrasions; medial distal metaphyseal femoral irregularities;
and subperiosteal cortical defects.11
Patient Presentation
Most commonly involves the medial distal femoral condyle
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
18/48

If the medial head of the gastrocnemius is involved, the lesion is recognized on the
posteromedial femoral condyle.
If the adductor magnus tendon is involved, the lesion appears on the medial distal femur.
Radiographic Appearance
AP radiographs demonstrate a well-circumscribed radiolucent lesion in the medial distal
femoral condyle.
CT scans show a small cortical defect with a geographic sclerotic border12 (Figure 15).
Figure 15 Images of a knee of a patient with nonossifying fibroma. A, AP radiograph
demonstrates a nonossifying fibroma of the distal femur. Note the sclerotic margin and the
narrow zone of transition to normal bone. B, Axial CT scan obtained because of concern for
the integrity of the posterolateral cortex of the distal femur. (Reproduced from Betsy M,
Kupersmith LM, Springfield DS: Metaphyseal fibrous defects. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2004;12[2]:89-95.)
MRI demonstrates a low signal intensity border on T1-weighted and T2-weighted images. The
lesion itself has low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and has a moderate-to-high signal
intensity on T2-weighted images.
Acute trauma may demonstrate a more aggressive MRI appearance because of marrow and
soft-tissue edema.
Management
Requires only recognition
Symptoms are self-limiting; therefore, no management is recommended.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
19/48

Subperiosteal Hematoma
Two primary etiologies of subperiosteal hematoma exist, including traumatic and atraumatic
causes in patients with neurofibromatosis or inherited coagulopathies, such as hemophilia
(Figure 16).
Figure 16 Clinical photograph shows a left thigh hematoma after a spontaneous bleed.
(Reproduced from Vanderhave KL, Caird MS, Hake M, et al: Musculoskeletal care of the
hemophiliac patient. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[9]:553-63.)
Trauma causes separation of the periosteum from the underlying bone, which results in
bleeding from nutrient vessels.
Blood accumulates deep to the periosteum.
Most common in skeletally immature patients
These may ossify over time and present as a smooth, benign-appearing cortical thickening
(Figure 17).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
20/48

Figure 17 AP radiograph of a right femur demonstrates lytic destruction of the middle to distal
femur secondary to pseudotumor. Large soft-tissue masses of the thigh show no internal
calcification or ossification. The remaining bones proximally and distally are severely
demineralized. (Reproduced with permission from Vanderhave KL, Caird MS, Hake M, et al:
Musculoskeletal care of the hemophiliac patient. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[9]:553-63.)
Infection
Acute Hematogenous Osteomyelitis
Patient Presentation
Most commonly presents as acute to subacute onset of fever, localized pain, and an antalgic
gait in skeletally immature children.13
Elevated inflammatory markers, specifically ESR and C-reactive protein level, are more
sensitive than leukocytosis.
Imaging Studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
21/48

Radiographic findings often are subtle, especially early in the disease process because
osteolysis and a periosteal reaction may take weeks to develop (Figure 18).
Figure 18 Radiographs demonstrate osteomyelitis. A, Lateral radiograph of the tibia and fibula
of a 7-year-old girl demonstrates osteomyelitis of the fibula. Note the lamellar periosteal
reaction, saucerization of the posterior cortex, and permeative bone destruction, which are
similar to the findings of Ewing sarcoma. B, AP radiograph of the femur of a 14-year-old boy
demonstrates chronic osteomyelitis. Note the solid periosteal new bone formation along most
of the bone. The small cortical break represents the location of the intramedullary infection
breaking out into the soft tissues (better observed on MRI; not shown). (Adapted from Avedian
RS: Pseudotumors and tumorlike lesions, in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds. Orthopaedic Knowledge
Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 43-55.)
MRI reveals areas of low signal intensity within the bone and soft tissues on T1-weighted
images and a hyperintense signal intensity within the infected bone or associated abscess and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
22/48

edema within the surrounding marrow on T2-weighted/STIR images (Figure 19).
Contrast enhancement often is present in the surrounding marrow and along the peripheral
rim of osseous or extraosseous abscesses.
Figure 19 Axial T2-weighted MRI of a lower leg shows cortical disruption of the fibula with an
associated large soft-tissue abscess and surrounding edema that may mimic the appearance
of bone sarcoma. (Reproduced from Avedian RS: Pseudotumors and tumorlike lesions, in
Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds. Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 43-55.)
Management
Appropriate, culture-specific antibiotic therapy is the cornerstone of the management of acute
hematogenous osteomyelitis.
Surgical débridement has a role in the management of subperiosteal or intraosseous
abscesses, sequestrum, concurrent septic arthritis, and failed antibiotic therapy.
Chronic Osteomyelitis
Patient Presentation
Often presents as chronic pain or open, draining wounds after fixation of fractures or
prosthetic joint replacements14 (Figure 20 and 21).
Patients typically do not present with signs of overwhelming infection and often do not have
leukocytosis.
Inflammatory markers (ESR/C-reactive protein level) frequently are elevated.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
23/48

Figure 20 Clinical photograph of the leg of a man with an open fracture and type I
osteomyelitis of the distal femur shows a draining fistula at the medial knee (arrow). The
patient underwent intramedullary fixation of the femur more than 20 years ago. (Reproduced
from Forsberg JA, Potter BK, Cierny G, Webb L: Diagnosis and management of chronic
infection. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19[suppl 1]:S8-S19.)
Figure 21Clinical photograph of a leg with type II osteomyelitis of the distal femur shows two
sinus tracts at the lateral knee (black arrows), near the tip of a partially failed free flap (white
arrow), 2 years after resection and postoperative radiation therapy for liposarcoma.
(Reproduced from Forsberg JA, Potter BK, Cierny G, Webb L: Diagnosis and management of
chronic infection. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19[suppl 1]:S8-S19.)
Imaging Studies
Radiographs and MRI may demonstrate a periosteal reaction, sequestrum, or evidence of a
draining sinus tract (Figure 22 and 23).

9/4/26, 10:49 AM
AAOS | Tumorlike Tumors and Pseudotumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000520
24/48

Figure 22 Images of the distal femur of a man with an open fracture and type I osteomyelitis.
A, Lateral radiograph demonstrates the healed fracture (white arrow) and possible sequestra
distally (black arrows). B, Axial T1-weighted MRI with contrast shows a medial sinus (solid
arrow). The dashed arrow indicates the medullary nidus. (Reproduced from Forsberg JA, Potter
BK, Cierny G, Webb L: Diagnosis and management of chronic infection. J Am Acad Orthop Surg

Pathophysiology
Paget disease of bone is caused by a disorder of skeletal remodeling with increased
osteoclastic resorption and increased bone remodeling. This creates highly vascular bone with
compromised integrity.

Inactive/sclerotic phase
Characterized by osteoblastic bone formation resulting in cortical thickening and trabecular

Epidemiology
Most commonly affects men older than 50 years, primarily of European descent
Patient Presentation
Most patients are asymptomatic, and Paget disease often is identified incidentally; however,
patients may present with pain, headaches, or deformity.
Headaches are secondary to calvarial involvement/compression of the cranial nerves.
Fractures may be secondary to uncoupled bone remodeling and structure compromise.
Degenerative arthritis frequently develops in patients with Paget disease.
Laboratory Findings
Characterized by elevated serum bone-specific alkaline phosphatase level and elevated urine
telopeptide level.
Radiographic Findings

Management
Diphosphonates
Halting the rapid bone remodeling via diphosphonate therapy leads to decreased pain and
stalls progression of the disease. In addition, it may decrease bleeding that occurs in patients
undergoing elective surgery (arthroplasty) to manage complications associated with Paget
disease.
Surgical management of orthopaedic manifestations
Degenerative joint disease is common in patients with Paget disease of bone and may
necessitate joint arthroplasty. Additional surgical management focuses on the management
of fractures or nerve compression secondary to Paget disease of bone.
Rarely, patients with a history of Paget disease may have new/worsening pain, which should
increase concern for Paget sarcoma, an aggressive secondary malignancy.
Hyperparathyroidism
Etiology
Elevated serum parathyroid hormone levels, from primary or secondary reasons, stimulate
bone resorption.
During rapid bone resorption, granulation tissue may form with fibrous tissue that replaces
bone.
Histologically, lesions contain hemosiderin-laden giant cells, giving it the brown tumor name.
Patient Presentation
Because of routine laboratory evaluation, patients with primary hyperparathyroidism rarely
present with osseous manifestations.
If symptomatic, patients present with bone pain and focal areas of subperiosteal bone
resorption, distal clavicle osteolysis, bone cysts, and brown tumors.15

Etiology
Pseudotumors are part of the spectrum of adverse tissue reactions in response to wear
particles after total hip arthroplasty, particularly with metal-on-metal bearings.

Etiology
In metal-on-metal implants, the particle size is exceedingly small compared with
polyethylene particles; however, particles may lead to pseudotumors. In addition, metal
hypersensitivity may play a role in the formation of pseudotumors in patients with a
metal-on-metal implant. These masses are reactive in nature; however, because of the
size and defined mass-like appearance, they often are mistaken for a tumor.
Pseudotumors represent foreign body granulomatous lesions, and occasionally may be
destructive. They may be fluid filled or solid. Occasionally, these reactions may be severe
and associated with considerable periarticular soft-tissue and osseous damage.
Imaging Studies
Early on, radiographs may demonstrate focal, punched-out osteolytic areas involving the
calcar.
MRI with metal artifact–reducing sequences allows for visualization of a peri-implant soft-
tissue mass.
The peripheral rim of the mass appears as low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and
frequently lacks enhancement with contrast. A heterogenous signal intensity often is observed
on T2-weighted images, with areas of hyperintensity and hypointensity compared with muscle.
Management
Appropriate evaluation for other causes of pain after total hip arthroplasty is critical to ensure
appropriate definitive surgical management is performed; most importantly, periprosthetic
infection should be ruled out. Revision total hip arthroplasty is the preferred treatment option;
however, soft-tissue compromise is associated with poorer outcomes.

A common finding in patients with osteoarthritis includes the formation of subchondral cysts;

Infection
Infection is a common reason for orthopaedic inpatient consultations. Frequently, the
suspicion for infection is high based on the patient history or the clinical scenario; however,
this is not always the case.
Intramuscular Abscess
Intramuscular abscesses may present as painful, large intramuscular masses similar to soft-
tissue sarcomas.
Patients have elevated inflammatory markers, leukocytosis, erythema, and fluctuance; in
addition, CT and/or MRI show a fluid-filled mass with peripheral contrast enhancement
without areas of nodularity or solid components.
On MRI, an abscess appears as an increased signal intensity on T2-weighted images and a low
signal intensity on T1-weighted images.
Internal heterogeneity may be observed if necrotic debris is present.
If the diagnosis remains unclear, image-guided aspiration/biopsy or open biopsy may be
performed before definitive management of the abscess via débridement, irrigation, and
antibiotic agents.
Myositis
Pyogenic myositis often presents in a manner similar to that of other infections, with pain,
elevated inflammatory markers, and systemic signs of infection.
Dissimilar from intramuscular abscesses, myositis presents as diffuse intramuscular edema,
which characterized by muscular enlargement and a high signal intensity on T2-weighted
contrast-enhanced MRIs.
Dissimilar from an abscess or tumor no identifiable fluid collection or mass is observed, and
the muscle fibers can be observed within the area of edema.
Frequently, these changes do not respect compartments and fascial planes, providing
additional evidence against a sarcoma diagnosis.

Although bacterial infection is a common cause of myositis (often associated with an
intramuscular abscess), other causes include viral infection, autoimmune disease, radiation
therapy, and trauma.
Management is directed at the underlying cause, and surgical management rarely is indicated.
Diabetic Myonecrosis
Patients with diabetes mellitus may present with the acute-onset extremity pain and swelling,
initially increasing suspicion for an acute infection.
Patients with diabetic myonecrosis do not have signs of systemic infection; white blood cell
count is normal, and fever is absent.
MRI demonstrates muscle and fascial edema, with hyperintensity observed on T2-
weighted/STIR images and areas of central hypointensity that do not enhance with contrast
and are consistent with necrosis.
Commonly multifocal within the same muscle
Thought to develop secondary to microvascular compromise and subsequent muscle necrosis
Managed nonsurgically; surgical management is associated with poorer outcomes19
Hematoma
Intramuscular hematomas may present in a manner similar to that of soft-tissue sarcomas as
a painless soft-tissue mass.
Hemorrhage leading to hematoma formation may be associated with traumatic, inherited, or
acquired coagulopathy or tumor-associated necrosis.
Similar to infection, benign hematomas typically do not respect fascial planes; if traumatic,
ecchymosis commonly is appreciated on clinical examination.
In pediatric patients, inherited hemophilia is a common cause of coagulopathy; in adults,
acquired coagulopathy secondary to anticoagulation via coumadin and other oral
anticoagulant agents (eg, rivaroxaban, apixaban) is a common presentation.
Tumor-associated hemorrhage rarely presents as ecchymosis or hemorrhage beyond the
anatomic compartment.20
Imaging studies may be very helpful in differentiating intramuscular hematoma from
neoplastic (benign and malignant) soft-tissue masses.
MRI is very helpful in differentiating hematoma from other solid soft-tissue masses or fluid-
filled cysts.

Hematoma
The appearance of a hematoma on MRI evolves with time as hemoglobin is broken
down. Acutely (hours to days old), hematomas appear as homogenous masses that are
isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and hypointense to muscle on T2-weighted
images. Conversely, subacute (1 week to 3 months) and chronic (>3 months) hematomas
appears as an increased signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images, with the
peripheral rim evolving from a high signal intensity to a low signal intensity with time.
Gradient echo sequences also may be particularly helpful in identifying hemoglobin.21
This evolution in imaging characteristics is because of the breakdown of hemoglobin to
deoxyhemoglobin and methemoglobin and the intracellular versus extracellular location
of these products. Spontaneous hematomas in patients without a history of trauma
should be scrutinized carefully for evidence of nodular enhancing masses internally or
along the periphery of the hematoma.
Tumoral Calcinosis
Tumoral calcinosis is a metabolic disorder that results in the deposition of calcium phosphate
in the periarticular soft tissues.
It most commonly affects the hips, shoulder, and elbows.
The underlying metabolic derangement in these patients is related to disruption of calcium
and phosphate hemostasis, which is regulated by the interplay between the renal,
gastrointestinal, and skeletal systems.
Inherited and acquired forms exist, which are differentiated based on serum laboratory
abnormalities.
Patient presentation may be variable, from minimal symptoms to severe, disabling pain and
loss of function.
Radiographically, periarticular soft-tissue mineralization is present in a confluence and lobular
pattern (Figure 33).
